title: They didn’t just betray Joseph.
paragraphs: They didn’t just betray Joseph.
They priced him.
Twenty pieces of silver.

That’s what his brothers decided a human life was worth. Their own brother. Their own blood. The same boy who once shared their table, laughed in their tents, and walked the same dusty hills of Canaan.

Genesis 37 begins like a quiet family story…
but it explodes into one of the darkest betrayals in the Bible.
Joseph was seventeen. Young. Favored by his father Jacob. The coat his father gave him wasn’t just clothing—it was a symbol. A declaration. A visible sign of love and blessing.
And his brothers hated it.
Scripture says their hatred grew so deep “they could not speak peacefully to him.” (Genesis 37:4)
Then came the dreams.

Joseph dreamed that their sheaves bowed to his.
He dreamed the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him.

These dreams were not arrogance.
They were God’s preview of the future.
But when jealousy listens to prophecy, it hears threat instead of promise.
So when Joseph came looking for his brothers in the fields of Dothan… they saw him coming from a distance.
And hatred started whispering.
“Here comes this dreamer.”
“Let’s kill him.”

Imagine that moment.
The sky over Dothan.
The wind over the dry hills.
And a group of brothers plotting murder before Joseph even arrived.
One brother, Reuben, tried to stop them from shedding blood. So they did something just as cruel.
They stripped him.
They took the robe his father had given him.
And they threw him into a pit.

No water.
No escape.
Just darkness.
Genesis doesn’t record Joseph’s cries here—but later Scripture reveals something heartbreaking.
In Genesis 42:21, the brothers admit:
“We saw the distress of his soul when he begged us, and we did not listen.”
Let that sink in.
Joseph was screaming for mercy.
And they sat down to eat.
Then opportunity came walking across the desert.
A caravan of Ishmaelites heading to Egypt.
And Judah had an idea.
“Why kill him when we can profit from him?”
That sentence reveals the true nature of sin.

Sin doesn’t just destroy.
Sometimes it monetizes betrayal.

So they pulled Joseph from the pit…
not to rescue him…
but to sell him.
Twenty pieces of silver.
Joseph disappeared down a desert road in chains.
Meanwhile, the brothers dipped his robe in goat’s blood and brought it to their father. When Jacob saw it, he believed Joseph had been devoured by a wild animal.
The family was shattered.

A father mourned.
A son was enslaved.
And the guilty brothers carried a secret that would haunt them for decades.
But here is the stunning truth hidden inside Genesis 37:
God is not mentioned as speaking in the chapter… yet He is still sovereign over every moment.
The pit did not cancel Joseph’s calling.
The chains did not cancel God’s plan.
The betrayal did not cancel the dream.
Years later Joseph himself would say the words that unlock the entire story:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” (Genesis 50:20)

That verse is not denial of pain.
It is the triumph of divine sovereignty over human sin.
And Joseph’s story whispers forward to someone greater.
Another beloved Son would come.

Like Joseph, He would be rejected by His own people.
Like Joseph, He would be betrayed for silver.
Like Joseph, He would be handed over to suffering by those who should have honored Him.
His name is Jesus Christ.
But unlike Joseph, Jesus was perfectly innocent.
He didn’t just suffer betrayal.
He carried the full weight of humanity’s sin on the cross.
And while Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver, Jesus was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver by Judas Iscariot.
Yet what looked like the greatest evil in history became the greatest act of redemption.
Through the cross, God turned betrayal into salvation.
Through the resurrection, God proved that darkness never gets the final word.
So if you feel like Joseph today…

Misunderstood.
Betrayed.
Thrown into a pit you didn’t choose.
Remember this:
The pit is not the end of the story.
God works in places that feel abandoned.
God writes redemption through moments that feel like defeat.
And in Christ, even what others meant to destroy you can become part of the testimony God uses to save lives.
Joseph’s chains eventually led to a palace.
But Jesus’ cross leads to something even greater:
forgiveness, new life, and eternal hope for anyone who repents and believes.
So here’s the question that turns this ancient story into a personal one:

Are you still holding onto the betrayal…
or are you ready to trust the God who can turn pits into purpose?

Because the same God who was with Joseph in the pit…
is the same God who raised Jesus from the grave.
And that means redemption is never impossible.
Not for Joseph.
Not for you.
And not for the people who hurt you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
